summary: Disodium edetate (edetate disodium, disodium EDTA) is a chelating agent given by slow intravenous infusion that binds calcium ions to form a soluble, renally excreted complex, thereby lowering serum calcium. Its appropriate use is limited to emergency treatment of selected hypercalcaemic states and control of ventricular arrhythmias associated with digitalis (digoxin) toxicity, where rapid reduction of ionised calcium is required. It must be infused slowly and well diluted because rapid administration or overdose can cause a dangerous, even fatal, fall in calcium with tetany, seizures, arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. It is nephrotoxic and is contraindicated in significant renal impairment or anuria. Edetate DISODIUM must not be confused with edetate calcium disodium (used for lead poisoning); disodium edetate is NOT indicated for atherosclerosis, peripheral/coronary artery disease or age-related degenerative conditions, where it offers no proven benefit and carries serious risk.

moa: Disodium edetate (EDTA) is a polyaminocarboxylic acid that forms stable, water-soluble chelate complexes with divalent and trivalent metal cations. Given intravenously it preferentially binds ionised calcium, lowering the concentration of free serum calcium; the calcium-EDTA complex is then excreted by the kidneys. This rapid reduction in ionised calcium underlies its use in hypercalcaemic emergencies and in digitalis-associated ventricular arrhythmias (where reducing calcium counteracts digitalis effects). Because it also binds other metals (e.g. zinc, magnesium), excessive or rapid use can disturb these as well.

absolute: Use for atherosclerosis or other unapproved indications
relative: Cardiac disease where abrupt calcium shifts are hazardous
Active or latent seizure disorders (tetany/seizure risk with hypocalcaemia)
monitor: Serum and ionised calcium (very frequently during infusion)
Blood pressure and other electrolytes (potassium, magnesium)

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established; disodium edetate chelates calcium and other essential metals (e.g. zinc) and could affect the mother and fetus. It should be used only if clearly necessary for a serious indication and the potential benefit outweighs the risk.
lact: There are limited data on use during breastfeeding. Given its potential to chelate essential metals, it should be used with caution and only when clearly indicated.
renal: Disodium edetate and its calcium complex are eliminated by the kidneys and the drug is nephrotoxic. It is contraindicated in anuria and significant renal impairment; renal function must be checked before and monitored during treatment, and dosing limited to reduce tubular injury.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is described for hepatic impairment; monitor the patient's overall status and electrolytes.

major: Digitalis/digoxin - by lowering calcium, disodium edetate alters digitalis effects; used deliberately in digitalis arrhythmia but requires careful ECG/calcium monitoring
Other agents that lower calcium or prolong QT - additive risk of hypocalcaemia and arrhythmia
moderate: Drugs whose activity depends on divalent cations may be affected by chelation
Concurrent nephrotoxic drugs - additive renal injury
minor: May reduce serum zinc, magnesium and other trace metals with repeated use
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant to acute parenteral use
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers measured serum/ionised calcium and may reduce magnesium/zinc; can affect tests dependent on calcium

common: Reactions at the infusion site (pain, phlebitis)
serious: Severe hypocalcaemia causing tetany, seizures, arrhythmias and cardiac arrest (especially with rapid infusion/overdose) - can be fatal
rare: Bone marrow depression with prolonged use
emergency: Acute severe hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures or arrhythmia/cardiac arrest

counsel: This medicine is given slowly into a vein in hospital to lower a dangerously high calcium level or to treat a specific heart-rhythm problem
You will be closely monitored with heart tracing and blood tests during the infusion
Tell staff at once of tingling around the mouth or fingers, muscle cramps/spasm, dizziness or palpitations
This is not a treatment for blocked arteries or ageing - it is only for specific emergencies
It is different from the calcium-EDTA used for lead poisoning
Report reduced urine output or swelling, which may indicate a kidney problem
pk: Serum calcium begins to fall during the infusion
Maximal calcium-lowering effect during/around the end of the slow infusion
Short plasma half-life; the agent and its calcium complex are rapidly cleared by the kidneys
Effect is transient; serum calcium may rebound, so repeated/monitored dosing may be needed
Store concentrate at room temperature; dilute before use and discard unused diluted solution per label
pearls: HIGH-RISK: rapid infusion or overdose can cause fatal hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest) - always dilute and infuse slowly with ECG and calcium monitoring
Edetate DISODIUM is NOT the same as edetate calcium disodium (lead poisoning) - confusing them can be lethal
Nephrotoxic - contraindicated in anuria/significant renal impairment; monitor renal function
NOT indicated for atherosclerosis, coronary/peripheral artery disease or age-related conditions - no proven benefit, serious risk
Keep calcium salts available to treat acute hypocalcaemia from overshoot
missed: Disodium edetate is given by a healthcare professional during acute treatment, not self-administered, so missed-dose instructions do not apply; the treating team manages timing and any repeat infusions.
overdose: Overdose or too-rapid infusion causes acute severe hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias and possible cardiac arrest, and can be fatal; renal damage may also occur. Stop the infusion immediately and give intravenous calcium (e.g. calcium gluconate) to correct hypocalcaemia, provide ECG and respiratory support, manage seizures, and monitor and support renal function.
